messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

For fifteen years, Omar had been the paramedic you wanted to see when your world fell apart. Calm, competent, and kind, he had a steady hand and a reassuring presence that could bring order to the most chaotic scenes. That all changed seven months ago, on a rain-slicked Tuesday afternoon when the dispatcher called out an MVC on the interstate. He didn't know until he was kneeling on the wet asphalt, the smell of gasoline and antiseptic wipes filling his nostrils, that the teenager trapped in the driver's seat was his own son, Amir. He worked on him with a desperate, automatic focus, the sights and sounds of the extrication blurring into a nightmare. There are parts of that hour he simply cannot remember, blank spaces where the terror was too immense to form a coherent memory. What he does recall returns not as a thought but as a full-body experience: the specific angle of Amir’s broken arm, the cold feel of the rain, the scent of blood mixing with the sterile smell of the ambulance. Because these fragments returned with such sensory intensity, he began to see echoes of them everywhere; the smell from a first-aid kit or the sight of rain on a car windscreen could now bring the entire memory rushing back.

When Omar first returned to work, he believed he could push through it. Then, on a routine call for a construction worker who had fallen, the sight of the man’s compound fracture sent him reeling. In an instant, he was back on the interstate, the memory of his son’s injuries flooding him with such sensory reality that he could feel the phantom weight of the C-collar in his hands. The terror was identical, a cold wave that left him breathless and shaking. Each time an image from that day broke through with such force, it served as visceral proof for the thought that followed: a competent paramedic, a good father, would not be falling apart like this. It felt like a confirmation of his own profound failure. This sudden, vivid recall left him feeling intensely vulnerable, and for the rest of his shift, he was on high alert, his concentration shattered. He found himself constantly scanning his surroundings, choosing a seat in the breakroom that kept his back to a wall, a profound sense of threat having taken root where his confidence used to be. Feeling so profoundly unsafe, even in the familiar setting of his own station, was the most convincing proof he had that something inside him had broken beyond repair. This persistent feeling of danger also seemed to keep his mind primed for the worst, and on days when his vigilance was highest, the memories of the accident were hardest to keep at bay, as if his brain was rehearsing the trauma to prepare for the next one.

This feeling of being unsafe began to bleed into every corner of his life. He had come to believe that he had failed in his most fundamental duty, not just as a paramedic but as a father. The thought, *I should have protected him*, became a constant, corrosive presence in his mind. This conviction that he had failed made the world feel treacherous, and he started interpreting every unexpected event as a potential catastrophe. His wife placing a hand on his shoulder as he stared out the window would cause him to jolt with alarm, a reaction that horrified them both. The sense of being permanently on guard made it impossible for the memories to stay buried; his hypervigilance seemed to actively seek out reminders of the accident, making it easier for the intrusive images to break through. This constant state of threat served only to reinforce his belief that he was broken, as he felt that a normal person, a capable person, would not be living with this level of fear. He became convinced he couldn't rely on himself, that his instincts were broken and he was permanently damaged by what had happened. This conviction that he was fundamentally compromised meant that things he would have once dismissed—a distant siren, a car backfiring—now snagged his attention, each one feeling like a potential sign of another disaster he would be helpless to prevent.

His entire life is now organized around managing these intrusions and the overwhelming feelings they bring. The belief that he is no longer reliable has made his paramedic's uniform feel like a costume he is unworthy to wear, and he has started calling in sick, unable to face the possibility of failing another patient. His avoidance of the hospital has ironically made it a more powerful trigger; now, even driving past the building or seeing a picture of an ambulance can feel like a direct confrontation with his perceived failure. The antiseptic smell of the hospital, or even seeing a news report about an accident, functions as a powerful trigger, bringing on a fresh wave of memories and a spike in his vigilance. It is on days when he encounters one of these reminders that he is most likely to call in sick, or to start a new, physically punishing project at home, a desperate attempt to outrun the internal chaos the trigger has unleashed. In response to this onslaught from both his own mind and the outside world, he tries desperately to keep his thoughts at bay. He throws himself into grueling tasks around the house—demolishing a bathroom, building a deck—working until his body aches too much for his mind to race.

However, these attempts at control have only tightened the trap. The more he tries to suppress the thoughts of the accident, the more forcefully they erupt as sensory-laden flashbacks, his mind refusing to let go of the details he most wants to forget. His avoidance of work serves as daily proof of his own negative appraisal: each missed shift confirms his fear that he can't rely on himself anymore. This exhaustion and the failure of his coping strategies have only heightened his sense of being under constant threat, making him even more susceptible to triggers. Last week, his wife cut her finger while cooking, and the sight of the blood on her skin sent a jolt of pure panic through him, the memory of his son’s more grievous wounds instantly present. Omar finally sought help after his wife found him sitting in their half-finished kitchen, staring blankly at the wall, unable to account for the last two hours. He is terrified that the calm, capable man he once was is gone for good, but a small part of him hopes that therapy might help him find a way to live with the ghosts of that rainy Tuesday, and to once again be the husband and father his family deserves.
